Blackbox is a sequential, reciprocal matchmaking prototype developed for The Sequential Matching Problem hackathon. It studies how a service should ask questions, choose introductions and manage availability when profiles are incomplete and feedback arrives late. Its purpose is to maximize completed dates followed by timely mutual interest. The complete project combines an interactive application with a separate, reproducible Python research package.

The official success definition is strict: a pair must complete its first date within 30 days of introduction, and both participants must record Yes to another meeting within three days of that date. Each benchmark episode has 200 members, 60 decision days and 40 follow-up days. Introductions, mutual acceptances, completed dates, eventual mutual interest and official qualifying successes are separate outcomes. High coverage alone does not demonstrate better matchmaking.

The active policy is conservative. It checks reciprocal hard requirements, including age preferences, who each member wants to meet, relationship structure, smoking, children, geography and schedule compatibility. A known incompatibility excludes a pair. Missing required information prevents automatic eligibility. Feasible pairs receive a score based on disclosed soft-preference agreements. The policy sorts candidates and greedily selects disjoint pairs, preventing overlapping assignments and repeated introductions. Its score is an agreement count, not a calibrated relationship-success probability.

Clarification precedes allocation. The policy identifies unresolved hard requirements among potentially compatible, available members and asks constraint questions within the available budget. It avoids repeatedly asking members who declined required information. After answers arrive, matching uses the refreshed observations. Unknown, declined and explicit negative answers remain different states. This preserves the distinction between missing information and actual incompatibility, although the conservative asking strategy is heuristic rather than a proven optimal information-acquisition policy.

The frontend provides Live matching, Matching pool, Results, Evidence, Architecture, Success cases, Failure cases and Activity views. Users can create a guided 24-member session or a generated 200-member session, select a scenario and seed, advance individual days, or run the simulation at different viewing speeds. Saved sessions can be restored. Member labels are synthetic identifiers; guided names are fictional. This prototype does not arrange dates or send messages to real people.

Explainability operates at two levels. Pair review shows reciprocal eligibility checks, disclosed attributes, individual soft-score contributions, candidate rank and competing selections. Results shows observed replies, date timing and qualification reasons. Shared, differing, unknown and declined attributes are displayed separately. New introductions retain decision-time profile snapshots. Older records expose only attributes disclosed by introduction time; missing historical rationale is acknowledged. Matching criteria explain selection, while feedback explains the recorded outcome; they do not establish someone's private reasons for accepting or rejecting.

The application backend contains the conservative JavaScript policy port, synthetic simulator, session store and API routes. Session endpoints create, restore, list and advance sessions; pair review is read-only. Private simulator truth, hidden biases and future events remain server-side. The browser receives disclosed profiles and already observed feedback. The JavaScript simulator uses a different random stream from the official Python simulator, so live application outcomes are never presented as additional official benchmark results.

Two hosting configurations are distinguished. The existing private Sites application uses a Cloudflare Worker, Sites identity and D1 storage. The standalone Vercel target uses Node.js Functions, a libSQL adapter and server-issued secure visitor cookies. Cookie identity isolates browser sessions; it is not account login. Production requires durable remote storage and deployment authentication. Atomic revision checks reject competing stale updates, request identifiers support retries without double advancement, and mutations enforce origin and request-size checks.

The offline research package contains training scripts, model assets, baselines, ablations, frozen experiment plans, machine-readable results and technical documentation. Its retained training collection comprises 288 simulator episodes and 21,367 mature introduced-pair observations, including 612 auxiliary mutual-interest positives and 224 official positives. Experimental models estimate success and availability costs. The coordinated controller connects questioning, matching and waiting through a shared objective, but remains a bounded planning approximation rather than an exact 60-day optimizer.

MLOps emphasizes reproducibility and guarded promotion. Training inputs and model assets have integrity checks; releases retain source and artifact identities. Training and evaluation use separate seeds, and hypothetical answers never become observed disclosures. Auxiliary eventual-interest labels support research without replacing official timely-success labels. Whole-game comparisons, uncertainty intervals, scenario regressions, service measures and runtime evidence govern promotion. A candidate with improved predictive loss can still remain undeployed when its actual policy benefit is unproven.

The original confirmation study contains 480 valid policy runs on 240 paired worlds: conservative produced 170 qualifying couples and coordinated produced 172. Across both policies, 242 runs achieved at least one official success and 238 scored zero. There were 342 qualifying couples altogether. The paired interval includes zero, so the two-couple advantage does not establish reliable superiority. These combined episode counts must not be described as one deployed policy's success rate.

The zero-score breakdown is 153 runs with qualifying-date mutual Yes but late feedback, 78 with completed dates without qualifying recorded mutual Yes, and seven without a completed first date. These describe observed outcomes, not proven psychological causes. The simulator draws feedback delays from one to five days; under independent uniform delays, both replies fall within three days with probability 36%. Reminders cannot improve simulated outcomes unless the simulator models their effect. The scoring rule must remain unchanged.

Historical case views now expose 35,837 pair records reconstructed across all 480 runs. Each replay reproduces the original action digest and outcome counts before acceptance. Reconstruction supplies traceable attributes and timelines; it is reproducibility evidence, not another independent evaluation. Local checks cover 1,200 simulated days, eligibility, budgets, hidden-data exclusion, results classification, UI flows, database isolation, idempotency and concurrent updates. Browser visual verification and native Windows/constrained Docker certification remain outstanding.

The latest application source is published on GitHub. Vercel deployment remains blocked by workspace authorization and requires a remote database connection. Further progress should focus on fresh on-policy training, stronger long-horizon evaluation, calibration and unequal-service analysis. The next release should demonstrate measurable improvements on fresh worlds while preserving reproducibility, legal actions and honest reporting. Conservative remains active until a replacement earns promotion through credible evidence.
